world: Tavish Orrenby is a second-year student at the fictional Tarnhollow University, taking three courses in Autumn term 2026: CNW 2140 Computer Networks (Dr. Oleska Brantigern), ECN 1620 Prices, Markets and Money (Prof. Tobiah Kessandru) and BIO 1380 Cells, Energy and Heredity (Dr. Maelis Underhaye). His Lecture-mode reference files are the lecture 7 slide deck on TCP congestion control, the networks lecturer's running notes on DNS and HTTP with follow-ups from lecture 7, this year's and last year's CNW 2140 syllabus, the economics lecture 5 slides on inflation and monetary policy, the economics professor's notes on elasticity, this year's and last year's ECN 1620 formula sheet, and the biology lecture notes on cellular respiration and Mendelian genetics. Each lecturer uses course-specific conventions (an initial window of 2 segments and a 1,200-byte MSS; queries-only DNS counting; the midpoint method with positive elasticities; a 'classroom rule' with weights 0.5 and 0.25 and a neutral rate of 1%; 30 ATP per glucose; a marsh-beetle cross with R/r notation), their own worked examples, and a few loose statements that the notes later pin down. There is no syllabus for ECN 1620 or BIO 1380 in the pack. Everything is fictional.

files.title: CNW 2140 Lecture 7: TCP congestion control (slide deck with presenter remarks)

facts.statement: Lecture 7 of CNW 2140, on TCP congestion control, was given by Dr. Oleska Brantigern on Tuesday 29 September 2026.
In CNW 2140, cwnd and ssthresh are counted in segments, never in bytes.
In every worked example in CNW 2140 the MSS is 1,200 bytes.
The course's initial window (IW) is 2 segments (not 1 as in older textbooks, not 10 as on many current servers).
Time is counted in rounds, and one round is one RTT.
In slow start every ACK grows cwnd by one segment, so cwnd doubles each round.
The lecturer's reading of the name: slow start is slow to start, not slow to grow; the name contrasts it with pre-1988 senders that opened with the whole receiver window at once.
Slow start ends when cwnd reaches ssthresh or when a loss is detected, whichever comes first.
Clamp rule of the course: slow start never overshoots the threshold; next cwnd = min(2 x cwnd, ssthresh).
The lecturer describes slow start as the aggressive phase, not the cautious one.
The congestion avoidance slide says only: at or above ssthresh, additive increase, +1.
ssthresh is described as the sender's memory of roughly where trouble began last time.
doc_needles: memory of roughly where trouble began

facts.statement: After three duplicate ACKs the course rule is: ssthresh = cwnd / 2, then cwnd = ssthresh, and the sender carries on in congestion avoidance.
After a retransmission timeout the course rule is: ssthresh = cwnd / 2, then cwnd = IW, and the sender goes back to slow start.
Halves are rounded down and ssthresh is never set below 2 segments.
Course simplification: the 3-segment window inflation of full Reno fast recovery is skipped; the window lands on the new ssthresh in one move.
The lecture 7 trace starts with IW = 2 segments, initial ssthresh = 16 segments, MSS = 1,200 bytes and RTT = 80 ms.
In the trace, rounds 1 to 4 are slow start with cwnd 2, 4, 8 and 16.
In the trace, rounds 5 to 8 are congestion avoidance with cwnd 17, 18, 19 and 20.
Three duplicate ACKs arrive in round 8 of the trace; round 9 has cwnd = 10 and ssthresh = 10.
In the trace, cwnd is 11 in round 10 and 12 in round 11, and the retransmission timer expires in round 11.
After the timeout in the trace, round 12 has cwnd = 2 and ssthresh = 6.
After the timeout the trace goes cwnd 4 in round 13, 6 in round 14 (clamped at ssthresh) and 7 in round 15 (congestion avoidance).
Lab 3 starts from the lecture 7 trace and asks students to extend it by ten rounds.
In the sawtooth the window swings between W / 2 and W, where W is the window at which loss occurs, so the average window is 0.75 x W.
The throughput formula used in the course is throughput = 0.75 x W x MSS / RTT.
Slide example: W = 20 segments, MSS = 1,200 bytes, RTT = 80 ms gives an average window of 15 segments, 18,000 bytes per round, 225,000 bytes per second, 1.8 Mbit/s.
The course does not use the square-root loss formula (Mathis and colleagues); it is on the further reading list only.
Smoothed RTT is updated as SRTT = 7/8 x SRTT + 1/8 x sample.
The timeout value is RTO = SRTT + 4 x RTTVAR.
Slide example: SRTT = 80 ms and RTTVAR = 15 ms give RTO = 140 ms.
Each time the retransmission timer expires, the RTO doubles (exponential backoff).
Course convention: exercises ignore the 1-second minimum RTO that real stacks apply.
The lecturer's picture for AIMD is the staircase and the cliff: climb one step per round, fall half the height on a loss.
The AIMD slide states, without qualification, that AIMD is fair.
Lecture 8 is TCP reliability and retransmission; the reading is Halloway and Minch, sections 6.3 to 6.5.
The lecture opens with the 1986 collapse story: throughput between two sites 400 yards apart fell from 32 kbit/s to 40 bit/s.
RTT variation is updated as RTTVAR = 3/4 x RTTVAR + 1/4 x the absolute difference between SRTT and the sample.

must_not_infer: The slides do not mention CUBIC, BBR, ECN marking or any congestion control variant other than the simplified Reno-style rules.
The slides give no exam date, exam weight or lab deadline.
The slides do not say what '+1' on the congestion avoidance slide is counted per; the lecturer's notes do.

files.title: CNW 2140 lecturer's notes, weeks 3 and 4 (DNS, HTTP, follow-ups from lecture 7)

facts.statement: The lecturer's notes for lectures 5 to 7 were last edited on Wednesday 30 September 2026.
The name resolved in every DNS example of the course is portal.tarnhollow.example.
The campus recursive resolver in the example is at 10.40.0.53.
The authoritative server for the zone is ns1.tarnhollow.example.
In CNW 2140 a cold lookup costs 4 queries: laptop to campus resolver, resolver to root, resolver to TLD, resolver to authoritative.
Textbooks that give 8 for the same exchange count the replies as well; the course counts queries only.
The example returns an A record, 203.0.113.48, with a TTL of 300 seconds.
'Think five minutes' was not a rule about DNS: the 300 seconds belongs to this one record and was chosen by whoever runs the zone.
The NS records for tarnhollow.example carry a TTL of 86,400 seconds (one day).
A warm lookup within the TTL costs 1 query from the laptop and none upstream.
Once the A record has expired but the NS records are still cached, the resolver skips the root and the TLD and goes straight to ns1.
NXDOMAIN replies are cached; in the course's zone the negative-caching time is 900 seconds, taken from the SOA record.
www.tarnhollow.example is a CNAME for portal.tarnhollow.example and costs no extra query in the example, because the same authoritative server returns the CNAME and the A record in one reply.
'DNS is UDP' needs a footnote: queries use UDP port 53 by default, but a reply over 1,232 bytes (the course's limit) gets the TC flag and the resolver repeats the query over TCP.
Zone transfers between name servers always use TCP.
The Lab 4 sandbox resolver is at 10.40.0.54 and empties its cache every 60 seconds.
The timetable page is one HTML file plus 11 embedded objects (8 images, 2 scripts, 1 stylesheet): 12 objects in all.
Round-trip counting convention: opening a TCP connection costs 1 RTT, each request with its response costs 1 RTT, and TLS and transmission time are ignored until lecture 12.
In the HTTP lecture the RTT was 50 ms.
Non-persistent HTTP, one object at a time: 2 RTT per object, 24 RTT for the page, 1,200 ms.
Persistent HTTP without pipelining: 13 RTT for the page, 650 ms.

Parallel non-persistent connections: the HTML is fetched first on its own connection, then up to 6 connections at a time for the embedded objects, each batch costing 2 RTT; the total was left for students to work out.
In the demo the short address /tt replied 301 Moved Permanently and redirected to /timetable.
In the demo the second load of the stylesheet replied 304 Not Modified, because the browser sent If-None-Match with the ETag v7-a41c and the file had not changed.
The lecturer also showed a 503 from enrolment week, when the portal was overloaded.
The stylesheet carries Cache-Control: max-age=600, so the browser does not ask for ten minutes and then revalidates with the ETag.

'HTTP is stateless, full stop' was too strong: the protocol is stateless, but the portal knows the user because the browser sends the sid cookie with every request; the state lives in the cookie and the server's session store.
HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one connection, but one lost TCP segment still stalls every stream.
HTTP/3 over QUIC is lecture 12 and will not be on the midterm.
doc_needles: will not be on the midterm

facts.statement: '+1' on the congestion avoidance slide means plus one segment per round (per RTT), not per ACK; per ACK the growth is 1/cwnd of a segment.
In the throughput example, 20 is the peak window, the window at which the loss happens; not the average and not the starting value.
'AIMD is fair' means fair between flows with similar round-trip times; a flow with a shorter RTT ends up with the larger share.
According to the lecturer's notes of 30 September, the midterm covers everything up to and including lecture 7, and lecture 8 will be examined in the final only.

must_not_infer: The notes do not give the weight or the date of the midterm or of the final exam.
The notes do not say that the statement about midterm scope replaces the syllabus.
The notes do not state the total for the parallel-connection case; it was left as an exercise.
Nothing here says a 300-second TTL is typical of DNS records in general.

files.title: ECN 1620 Lecture 5: Inflation and monetary policy (slides)

facts.statement: Lecture 5 of ECN 1620, on inflation and monetary policy, was given by Prof. Tobiah Kessandru on Wednesday 30 September 2026.
The running case of the course is the small open economy of Norvale: currency the crown, central bank the Norvale Reserve Board (NRB).
ECN 1620 defines inflation as a sustained rise in the general price level.
doc_needles: rise in the general price level

facts.statement: In ECN 1620 'sustained' means lasting at least two consecutive quarters; a one-off jump in prices is a price-level shock, not inflation.
Course bands: mild is below 3% a year, moderate is 3% to below 10%, high is 10% a year or more, hyperinflation is 50% a month or more.
The Norvale student basket in base year 2024: rent 700, food 300, transport 90, phone and data 60, books 100; total 1,250 crowns.
The same basket cost 1,300 crowns in 2025 and 1,365 crowns in 2026.
Inflation in 2026 is 5.0% (from 104.0 to 109.2).
Inflation is always measured from the previous year's index, not from the base year.
In this course inflation means CPI inflation unless a problem says GDP deflator.
doc_needles: unless a problem says GDP deflator

facts.statement: The course's demand-pull example is the 2021 Norvale housing grant.
The course's cost-push example is the 2023 Port Selby harbour strike, which raised the cost of everything imported.
Quantity-equation example: Norvale's money supply grows 7%, velocity is flat, real output grows 2%, so predicted inflation is 5%.
Real rate = nominal rate - inflation is the approximation, used whenever inflation is below 10%; at 10% or more the exact form (1 + nominal) = (1 + real) x (1 + inflation) is used.
Example: a Norvale savings account pays 3.5%; with inflation at 5.0% the saver's real return is -1.5%.
The slide states, without saying which rate, that real rates are negative right now.
doc_needles: Real rates are negative right now.

facts.statement: The NRB's inflation target is 2%.
The NRB's policy rate today is 4.25%.
The Board meets 8 times a year.
The NRB's tools are the policy rate (the main one), open market operations, the reserve requirement (8% in Norvale) and forward guidance.
The classroom rule: policy rate = neutral real rate + inflation + 0.5 x (inflation - target) + 0.25 x output gap.
The classroom rule uses a neutral real rate of 1% and a target of 2%.
The classroom rule is a Taylor-type rule with the course's own weights; in ECN 1620 exams students use the classroom weights, not the numbers of Taylor's 1993 paper.
Norvale today: inflation 5.0%, output gap -2%; the classroom rule gives 7.0%.
The slide states that the NRB is behind the curve, without saying by how much or relative to what.
doc_needles: The NRB is behind the curve.

facts.statement: The course names four transmission channels: interest-rate, credit, exchange-rate and expectations.
Lags: borrowing responds within 1 to 2 quarters; the course's rule of thumb for the full effect on inflation is 6 quarters.
Money multiplier = 1 / reserve ratio; with Norvale's 8% it is 12.5.
Example: 200 crowns of new reserves can support up to 2,500 crowns of deposits.
Unexpected inflation moves wealth from lenders to borrowers.
Next week's lecture 6, on Wednesday 7 October, is unemployment and the Phillips curve.
Problem set 3 is due Wednesday 14 October.
The slides list shoe-leather costs and menu costs among the costs of inflation.

must_not_infer: The slides do not say which rate 'real rates are negative right now' refers to; the professor's notes do.
The slides do not give any ECN 1620 exam date or assessment weight.
The slides do not cover comparative advantage, trade, or the Phillips curve itself (only that it is next week's topic).

files.title: ECN 1620 professor's notes, lectures 3 to 5 (elasticity; follow-ups on inflation and monetary policy)

facts.statement: Prof. Kessandru's notes for lectures 3 to 5 were last edited on Thursday 1 October 2026.
Lecture 3 of ECN 1620, on elasticity, was on Wednesday 16 September 2026.
Every percentage change in an elasticity calculation in this course uses the midpoint method: the change divided by the average of the old and new values.
The professor's reason for the midpoint method: it gives the same number in both directions (price rise or price cut).
Price elasticity of demand is reported as a positive number in this course; the minus sign is dropped.
For cross-price and income elasticity the sign is kept because it carries the information.
Demand is elastic above 1, inelastic below 1, unit elastic at exactly 1.
Worked example 1: the campus cafe Brindle & Oat raised the price of a flat white from 3.00 to 3.60 crowns.
In worked example 1 daily sales fell from 440 cups to 360.
In worked example 1 the quantity change is 20% (80 on an average of 400) and the price change is 18.2% (0.60 on an average of 3.30).
In worked example 1 the elasticity is 1.10 and demand is elastic.
In worked example 1 revenue was 1,320 crowns a day before and 1,296 after; revenue fell when the price rose.
Worked example 2: the monthly bus pass rose from 38 to 42 crowns and sales fell from 1,050 passes to 950.
In worked example 2 the elasticity is 1.00 (unit elastic) and revenue is 39,900 crowns before and after.
The bus pass example was chosen to show a price rise that leaves revenue exactly where it was.
doc_needles: leaves revenue exactly where it was

facts.statement: The professor's mnemonic for the determinants of elasticity is SPLAT: substitutes, proportion of income, luxury or necessity, addictive or habitual, time.
Cross-price example: oat milk went up 10% and flat white sales fell 4%; cross-price elasticity is -0.4, complements.
Income example: student stipends rose 10% and instant noodle sales fell 3%; income elasticity is -0.3, an inferior good.
Tax example: a tax of 0.50 crowns per cup; buyers pay 0.30 more, sellers keep 0.20 less; buyers carry 60% of it.
The tax example shows that demand for coffee near campus is less elastic than supply.
'Elasticity is just the slope' was said too loosely and is wrong: on a straight-line demand curve the slope is the same everywhere but elasticity is above 1 at high prices and below 1 at low prices.

'Behind the curve' means the Board's actual policy rate is below the rate that the classroom rule prescribes for today's inflation and output gap; the distance between the two is how far behind it is.
'Real rates are negative right now' referred to the policy rate in real terms (the policy rate less current inflation), not to the savings account on the same slide.
doc_needles: not talking about the savings account

facts.statement: 'Always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon' is Friedman's line; the course's position is that in the long run sustained inflation needs money growth, and in the short run it can start from demand or from costs.
The 6 quarters lag is a rule of thumb for Norvale, not a law of nature; larger and more closed economies are usually slower.
Lecture 4 (market failure) has its own handout and is not covered in these notes.

must_not_infer: The notes do not state the numerical size of the 'behind the curve' gap or of the negative real policy rate; those need the slide values.
The notes do not cover comparative advantage or trade.
The notes give no ECN 1620 exam date or weight.

files.title: ECN 1620 formula sheet, version 2026.2

facts.statement: This is version 2026.2 of the ECN 1620 formula sheet, issued Monday 14 September 2026.
Students may bring one unmarked printed copy of the formula sheet to the midterm and to the final exam.
Percentage change = (new - old) / average of old and new, x 100: the midpoint method, used for every elasticity.
PED = % change in quantity demanded / % change in price, reported as a positive number.
doc_needles: Report PED as a positive number

facts.statement: Elastic: PED above 1; unit elastic: PED equal to 1; inelastic: PED below 1.
Cross-price elasticity keeps its sign: positive means substitutes, negative means complements.
Income elasticity keeps its sign: negative is an inferior good, between 0 and 1 a necessity, above 1 a luxury.
CPI in year t = cost of the basket in year t / cost of the basket in the base year, x 100.
Inflation rate = (CPI this year - CPI last year) / CPI last year, x 100.
Real rate = nominal rate - inflation when inflation is below 10%; at 10% or more the exact form (1 + nominal) = (1 + real) x (1 + inflation).
Money multiplier = 1 / reserve ratio.
Classroom rule: policy rate = neutral real rate + inflation + 0.5 x (inflation - target) + 0.25 x output gap.
The classroom rule uses a neutral real rate of 1% and a target of 2% unless told otherwise.
Rule of 70: years to double = 70 / annual growth rate in percent.
Rounding: elasticities to 2 decimal places.
Rounding: rates and percentages to 1 decimal place.
Round only at the end and carry at least four significant figures through the working.
The output gap is actual output less potential output, as a percentage of potential; a negative gap means producing below potential.
A bare number earns no method marks; the method must be stated in one line first.
Real value = nominal value / CPI, x 100.
Money amounts are rounded to whole crowns unless the problem is stated in cents.

files.title: BIO 1380 lecture notes, lectures 8 and 9 (cellular respiration; Mendelian genetics)

facts.statement: Dr. Maelis Underhaye's notes for BIO 1380 lectures 8 and 9 were posted on Friday 2 October 2026.
Lecture 8, on cellular respiration, was on Thursday 24 September 2026.
The four stages and their places: glycolysis in the cytosol; pyruvate oxidation and the citric acid cycle in the mitochondrial matrix; oxidative phosphorylation on the inner mitochondrial membrane.
The lecturer says 'citric acid cycle'; the course text calls it the Krebs cycle.
Glycolysis yields 2 ATP net (4 made, 2 spent) and 2 NADH per glucose.
Pyruvate oxidation yields 2 NADH and 2 carbon dioxide per glucose.
The citric acid cycle (two turns) yields 2 ATP, 6 NADH, 2 FADH2 and 4 carbon dioxide per glucose.
Exchange rates used in BIO 1380: 2.5 ATP for each NADH made inside the mitochondrion and 1.5 ATP for each FADH2.
Shuttle convention: the course assumes the glycerol-phosphate shuttle, so each of the 2 NADH from glycolysis is worth 1.5 ATP.
The course total is 30 ATP per glucose (2 + 3 + 5 + 2 + 15 + 3).
Older textbook figures of 36 or 38 must not be used in this course.
For each NADH, Complex I pumps 4 protons, Complex III pumps 4 and Complex IV pumps 2: 10 protons.
FADH2 hands its electrons to Complex II, which pumps nothing, so only 6 protons are pumped.
ATP synthase needs 4 protons per ATP: 3 to turn the rotor and 1 to bring the phosphate in.
Hence 10 / 4 = 2.5 ATP per NADH and 6 / 4 = 1.5 ATP per FADH2.
The lecturer's picture: the electron transport chain is a row of pumps filling a reservoir (the proton gradient); ATP synthase is the turbine in the dam wall; oxygen is the river below the dam.
Cyanide blocks Complex IV; in the dam picture the outflow gate is shut and the pumps stall.
DNP (2,4-dinitrophenol) is a hole in the dam wall: protons leak back without passing the turbine; oxygen use goes up, ATP output goes down, the energy leaves as heat.
Fermentation yields 2 ATP per glucose, all from glycolysis; its real job is to turn NADH back into NAD+ so glycolysis can keep running.
Yeast make ethanol and carbon dioxide; muscle cells make lactate.
The balloon flask demonstration: baker's yeast with 10 g of sucrose in 100 mL of water at 35 degrees C, a balloon over the neck; after 20 minutes the balloon stood upright; the gas is carbon dioxide.
'Oxygen is where the energy comes from' was said too quickly: oxygen is the final electron acceptor, the bottom of the hill, not the fuel.
'No oxygen, no ATP' is wrong as it stands: oxidative phosphorylation stops but glycolysis carries on making ATP.
Lecture 9, on Mendelian genetics, was on Thursday 1 October 2026.
The classroom organism is the marsh beetle: R (russet) is dominant over r (grey); S (spotted) is dominant over s (plain).
Notation in BIO 1380: the two alleles are written with a slash, dominant first, as in R/r; phenotype ratios are written with the dominant class first.
R/r x R/r gives genotypes 1 : 2 : 1 and phenotypes 3 : 1.
This year's class count for R/r x R/r was 152 offspring: 114 russet and 38 grey.
'Half of them are carriers' meant half of all the offspring are R/r; among the russet beetles alone, two-thirds are carriers.
A backcross to the recessive parent (R/r x r/r) gives 1 : 1 and is used to tell R/R from R/r; a single grey offspring shows the russet parent is R/r.
R/r S/s x R/r S/s, with the genes on different chromosomes, gives phenotypes 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.
In a brood of 320 the expected numbers are 180 russet spotted, 60 russet plain, 60 grey spotted and 20 grey plain.
The lecturer says 'partial dominance' where the course text says incomplete dominance; snapdragon red x white gives pink, and pink x pink gives 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white.
Hardy-Weinberg: p + q = 1 and p squared + 2pq + q squared = 1, where q squared is the frequency of the recessive phenotype.
Pond example: grey beetles are 16% of the pond population, so q = 0.4 and p = 0.6, and carriers (2pq) are 48%.
Dominant does not mean common: dominance describes how an allele shows in a heterozygote, not its frequency.
Fruit fly white eye is recessive and X-linked; carrier female x red-eyed male gives half of the sons white-eyed and none of the daughters.
doc_needles: half of the sons are white-eyed

facts.statement: Quiz 3 covers lectures 7 to 9 and takes the first 15 minutes of class on Thursday 8 October.
Lecture 10 of BIO 1380 is linkage and recombination.
The course text is Pellowe and Strand, Life at the Cell Scale; where the lecturer's wording differs, students use hers.

facts.statement: This is the second issue of the BIO 1380 practical handbook for Autumn 2026, dated Friday 4 September 2026.
There are four practicals, P1 to P4, each a single session of two and a half hours in the Wetherden Teaching Laboratory, room LS 0.19, at a bench of four people.
Practical groups: A Monday 09:10 to 11:40, B Monday 14:10 to 16:40, C Wednesday 09:10 to 11:40, D Wednesday 14:10 to 16:40; group lists are on the course site.
P1 (catalase and temperature) runs in the week beginning Monday 14 September and its short report is due Friday 25 September.
P2 (yeast fermentation on different sugars) runs in the week beginning Monday 28 September and its full report is due Monday 12 October, for all groups.
P3 (scoring marsh beetle crosses) runs in the week beginning Monday 12 October and its full report is due Friday 23 October.
P4 (osmosis in potato tissue) runs in the week beginning Monday 2 November and its full report is due Friday 13 November.
Over the term a student hands in four practical reports: one short report (P1) and three full reports (P2, P3, P4).
The short report belongs to P1 only: one side of A4 and at most 350 words.
Ottoline Varkess is the senior demonstrator; she runs every session and is in room LS 0.21.
Idris Penhallick is the laboratory manager: the room, the equipment, the lockers and lost property; room LS 0.23.
The demonstrators are postgraduate students, one to every three benches; they help at the bench and they mark the reports.
The risk checklist on the course site must be completed by 18:00 on the day before the session.
A missed session must be reported by email to the senior demonstrator within 2 working days; a catch-up session runs on the Friday of the same week, 14:10 to 16:40, with 12 places.
A demonstrator initials the results page of the notebook before the student leaves; the notebook itself is not handed in.
P1 uses water baths at 5, 20, 37, 55 and 75 degrees C; each tube is left for 8 minutes, the oxygen is read after 90 seconds, and there are three replicates at each temperature.
In P2 each tube gets 10 mL of yeast suspension and 10 mL of sugar solution made up at 50 g per litre; the five tubes are glucose, sucrose, maltose, lactose and a water control.
In P2 the tubes stand in a water bath at 32 degrees C and the gas is read at 10, 25 and 40 minutes.
For P3 the crosses were set up by the technicians in the teaching laboratory's insectary five weeks before the session, and the parents were taken out once the eggs had been laid.
In P3 tray 1 comes from a one-gene cross (both parents heterozygous for wing-case colour) and tray 2 from a two-gene cross (colour and spots).
doc_needles: Tray 1 comes from a one-gene cross
Tray 2 comes from a two-gene cross

facts.statement: P3 scoring rules: trays are chilled for seven minutes; a beetle counts as spotted with one clear spot or more on either wing case; a tray with fewer than 90 offspring is too small to analyse by itself.
P3 analysis: chi-square against the numbers the lecture's ratio predicts, degrees of freedom equal to the number of phenotype classes less one, at the 0.05 level, rounded to hundredths.

In P4 each bench cuts 18 cylinders trimmed to 40 mm, three for each of six sucrose solutions (0.00, 0.15, 0.25, 0.35, 0.55 and 0.80 mol per litre), leaves them for 55 minutes at room temperature and weighs to 0.01 g.
A full report is at most 1,400 words, not counting tables, figure legends and the reference list; a report that runs over is read as far as the limit.
doc_needles: read as far as the limit

facts.statement: Reports go in as a single PDF through the course site by 09:00 on the due date, which is the same for all four groups.
Demonstrators cannot change a deadline; a student who cannot meet one applies to the Life Sciences teaching office, room LS 1.02, before the deadline has passed.
doc_needles: Life Sciences teaching office, room LS 1.02

facts.statement: Reports are marked by the demonstrators and checked by the senior demonstrator; each comes back with a band (Excellent, Good, Sound, Weak or Incomplete) and comments under five headings.
doc_needles: Excellent, Good, Sound, Weak or Incomplete

facts.statement: A band thought to be wrong is raised with the senior demonstrator within 5 working days of the report being returned, bringing the report and the notebook.
Critical values of chi-square at the 0.05 level: 3.84 for 1 degree of freedom, 5.99 for 2, 7.81 for 3, 9.49 for 4 and 11.07 for 5.

Appendix C: breakages, locker keys and lost property go to the laboratory manager; a missed session, a change of group or a disputed band to the senior demonstrator; a deadline that cannot be met to the Life Sciences teaching office.
Students collect data as a bench and write their reports alone.

must_not_infer: The handbook does not give the temperature, or any other condition, at which the beetle broods were reared; every temperature in it belongs to a water bath of P1 or P2, or is room temperature in P4.
The handbook does not say how the practical reports count towards the BIO 1380 course mark.
The handbook states no penalty for a late report; it says only that demonstrators cannot change a deadline and where to apply.
The handbook does not say which practical group the student is in.
The handbook does not state the ratios expected in the beetle crosses; it refers to the lecture for them.

facts.statement: The class results sheet for BIO 1380 Practical 2 is sheet 2, compiled by O. Varkess on Monday 5 October 2026; sheet 1 lacked group D.
The sheet has one row for each tube on each bench: 32 benches from groups A to D, five tubes a bench, with the gas volume in mL at 10, 25 and 40 minutes.

Class mean for sucrose: 2.7 mL at 10 minutes, 10.2 mL at 25 minutes and 18.4 mL at 40 minutes.
Class mean for maltose: 0.3 mL at 10 minutes, 3.1 mL at 25 minutes and 9.7 mL at 40 minutes.
Class mean for lactose: 0.2 mL at 10 minutes, 0.5 mL at 25 minutes and 0.9 mL at 40 minutes.
Class mean for the water control: 0.2 mL at 10 minutes, 0.3 mL at 25 minutes and 0.5 mL at 40 minutes.

Version 1 allowed Python 3 only.

files.title: CNW 2140 Lab 4 handout (build a DNS resolver), version 2

facts.statement: This is version 2 of the CNW 2140 Lab 4 handout, issued Friday 9 October 2026; it replaces version 1 of Monday 5 October.
The lab builds a command-line resolver called tinyresolve that starts at the lab root, follows each referral and prints the address and the servers it asked.
Version 2 allows Python 3 or Go; library calls that resolve a name or pack and unpack DNS messages are not allowed.
The lab tree has its own root, one top-level zone called cnwlab and three zones under it: alder.cnwlab, birch.cnwlab and cedar.cnwlab.
The address of the lab root is in the file root.hint in the starter repository; the tree answers only on the lab subnet or over the lab VPN.
Address records in the lab tree carry a TTL of 40 seconds.
The student's resolver must not send its queries to the sandbox resolver or to the campus resolver; the sandbox is for comparing answers only.
doc_needles: must not send its queries there

facts.statement: Milestones M1 to M4: one query to the lab root; follow referrals; follow an alias for a chain of up to three aliases; keep a cache that respects the TTL.
doc_needles: chain of up to three aliases

facts.statement: In version 2 every lookup must finish within 3 seconds; a lookup that runs longer scores nothing for that name.
The resolver waits at most 750 ms for any one server and does not try the same server more than twice.
The resolver gives up after 9 referrals and prints FAIL with the reason.
According to the handout, no name in the published or the hidden list returns a truncated reply; the retry over TCP need not be implemented and is not marked.
doc_needles: You do not need to implement the retry over TCP

facts.statement: In version 2 the published list, names.txt, holds 15 names over the three zones, with two aliases and one name that does not exist.
The hidden list is a different set of names in the same three zones; the handout does not say how many names it holds.
doc_needles: We do not say how many names it holds

facts.statement: The grader looks every name up twice (cold cache, then straight afterwards) and, for the names that test expiry, a third time.
Students hand in the repository tagged lab4-final and, in version 2, a report of no more than three pages.
The handout leaves the due date, the hand-in time and the late rules as already published for the course's labs.
doc_needles: This handout does not change them.

facts.statement: Version 2 marking shares: published names 35%, hidden names 25%, cache behaviour (milestone M4) 15%, report 25%.
Version 2 lists the sections that changed since version 1 (language, time limit, published list, report length, marking shares) without printing the old values.

intentional_conflicts.other_value: a resolver without the retry will lose it

must_not_infer: The handout does not say how many names the hidden list holds, so no total running time for the hidden names can be worked out from it.
The handout does not state the due date, the weight or the late penalty of the lab; it points to what is already published.
The handout does not say that it overrides the lecturer's notes on truncated replies, and the notes do not say that they override the handout.

files.title: CNW 2140 lecturer's notes, week 5 (lecture 9: IP addressing and subnets)

facts.statement: The lecturer's notes for lecture 9 were last edited on Friday 9 October 2026.
Lecture 9 of CNW 2140 is on IP addressing and subnets; every address in the course comes out of the campus block 10.40.0.0/16.
House count: the number of usable hosts in a subnet is two raised to the number of host bits, less two (the subnet address and the broadcast address are taken off).

Campus plan: servers 10.40.0.0/24 (254 usable hosts), teaching labs in Hale-Voss 10.40.8.0/22 (1,022), staff offices 10.40.16.0/20 (4,094), halls of residence 10.40.64.0/18 (16,382), library and study rooms 10.40.128.0/23 (510).
Worked example A: the teaching labs' /22 is cut into four /24s, one for each lab room, with 254 usable hosts each.
Worked example B: a /28 has 16 addresses and 14 usable hosts, and one /24 holds 16 subnets of that size.
Worked example C: host 10.40.9.93 is in 10.40.9.0/24 (broadcast 10.40.9.255) and, with a /28, in 10.40.9.80/28.
A router takes the matching row with the longest prefix; a packet for 10.40.9.93 goes to Hale-Voss.
doc_needles: takes the row with the longest prefix

facts.statement: In this course an IP header is 20 bytes with no options; packets in the examples leave their host with a hop limit of 16, counted in routers passed and not in seconds.
The lab Ethernet has an MTU of 1,500 bytes and the old serial link to the Annex has an MTU of 620 bytes.

Fragmentation rules of the course: each fragment has a 20-byte IP header of its own; every fragment except the last carries a payload that is a multiple of 8 bytes and as much as the MTU allows; only the IP payload is cut, a TCP header (20 bytes, no options) included.
Fragments are put back together only at the destination host, never by a router on the way.
Slide example: a 1,500-byte packet for the Annex has a 1,480-byte payload that goes out as 600, 600 and 280: three fragments of 620, 620 and 300 bytes on the wire.
DHCP leases in the teaching labs last 90 minutes and leases in the halls last 12 hours.
Worked example D: three borrowed bits turn the halls' /18 into eight /21s, each with 2,046 usable hosts.

According to the lecturer's notes, the Lab 4 resolver must handle truncation by repeating the query over TCP: one of the hidden names checks exactly that, and a resolver without the retry will lose it.
doc_needles: One of the hidden names is there to check exactly that
a resolver without the retry will lose it

facts.statement: "A /24 has 256 hosts" was said too loosely: it has 256 addresses and 254 usable hosts.
In the demo, the trace from the lab room to the portal showed 5 routers on the way.

intentional_conflicts.this_value: a resolver without the retry will lose it

must_not_infer: The notes do not say that their remark on Lab 4 replaces the handout, and they do not mention the handout or its versions.
The notes state no segment size; the size of a full TCP segment in this course comes from the congestion control slides.
The notes do not explain how forwarding tables are built; that is left to the next lecture.
The notes say nothing about what any exam covers.
